newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary and Slovakia fight dam dispute in court.
newsitem.headline: Hungary and Slovakia fight dam dispute in court.

text.p: Hungary and Slovakia prepare to do battle on Monday in the Hague International Court to resolve a long-running dispute over Slovakia's Gabcikovo dam project diverting the river Danube, which forms the border between the two countries.

The controversial scheme was originally a joint venture between the then Czechoslovakia and Hungary but Budapest suspended work on its own dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 after pressure from environmental groups and then pulled out all together in 1992.

The episode has strained relations between Budapest and Bratislava since Slovakia, which took over the project when Czechoslovakia split in 1993, agreed to take the case to the International Court but ploughed on with the $500 million hydroelectric scheme at Gabcikovo.
"We agreed with Slovakia to put three questions to the court," head of Hungary's legal team Laszlo Valki told Reuters.

"Was Hungary entitled to abandon the project, was the then Czechoslovakia entitled to pursue the diversion of the Danube and what legal consequences does the Court draw from its answers to those questions?".

Hungary maintains it pulled out of the 1977 intergovernmental agreement because of environmental factors not taken into account in the original plan and says Slovakia's unilateral diversion of a common border violates international law.

At the end of 1995 the Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF) said the scheme was threatening up to 90 percent of the marshy region's rich plant and wildlife as the diversion of up to 90 percent of the Danube's flow to feed the giant plant caused ground water levels to drop by up to three metres (10 feet).
"Between 80 and 90 percent of the flood plain's internationally renowned plant and wild life is approaching extinction," Alexander Zinke, WWF's officer for Central and eastern Europe said.
The WWF added that an underground area of 14,000 cubic metres of water-filled gravel containing Europe's best and largest drinking water reserve was now threatened with pollution.
But Slovakia says Hungary has made the problem worse by illegally abandoning construction of the Nagymaros dam which would have compensated for the effects of Gabcikovo.
A senior Slovak official accused Hungary last week of conducting an "inappropriate propaganda campaign".
"The experts know that the Hungarian side cannot win," Julius Binder, director of Gabcikovo dam's general constructor Vodohospodarska Vystavba s.p., said.
"Hungarians say we had taken their water out, but that part of the Danube is neither Hungarian or Slovak, it is common water," he added.
Hungary will be the first to put its case to the court and has been given the whole of this week to do so.
Following a two-week recess Slovakia will have its turn, after which the judges of the Court will view both the dam site and the effects of the project on the Hungarian side.
"This will be the first time in its almost fifty year history the Court has left the Hague to consider evidence," Valki said.
Both sides have assembled international teams of lawyers and scientific experts to put their case.
The Court is expected to deliver its ruling on the case in the autumn and then the two sides will have six months to implement its recommendations.
"In a sense that will be the toughest part," one Hungarian government source said. "We then have to sit down after all this acrimony and thrash it out between us."
Recent talks by government experts on exploring a possible basis for an out-of-court settlement will continue, the sources said.
